scenarios.title: Spent six months building a feature the market had moved away from
scenarios.situation: We set out to build personalised dashboards for our analytics product: layouts that rearranged themselves around each user's habits, with automatically suggested reports. It was meant to underpin the product's future, but it took about six months with interruptions, and the business changed direction several times meanwhile.
scenarios.task: Deliver the feature and integrate it into the existing platform.
scenarios.action: I led the team through building the underlying engine and fitting it into the platform. We kept going as priorities shifted because the feature had been agreed as strategic, and we didn't stop to check whether that was still true.
scenarios.result: We shipped it, but by then customers had lost interest in the approach, so it added little value. Since then I set review points on long projects to ask whether the original reason still holds.

scenarios.title: Prepared engineering for its first security certification
scenarios.situation: Our largest customers began requiring a formal information-security certification. Engineering had little written process: no risk register, inconsistent logging, and coding standards that lived in people's heads.
scenarios.task: Get development and IT ready for the first audit, and set things up so the evidence kept itself up to date afterwards.
scenarios.action: I wrote the policies and procedures with the people who would follow them, introduced coding and security standards, set up central logging, and started a risk register we reviewed monthly. I worked through a few hundred control requirements with IT and the operations team. After the first audit, I focused on making evidence a by-product of normal work, such as tickets and pipeline logs, instead of a scramble before each audit.
scenarios.result: We passed the first audit, and by the second renewal preparing for it was routine. The team also became much clearer about handling personal data.
measurableResults: Passed the first certification audit and two renewals
After about nine months of preparation

scenarios.title: Moved a team from a few big releases a year to releasing every fortnight
scenarios.situation: When I joined, the team worked on large features for months at a time and released about three times a year. Testing happened at the end, and every release was a stressful, all-hands event.
scenarios.task: Help the team deliver smaller changes more often, and more safely.
scenarios.action: I introduced two-week iterations and spent time with the team breaking work into smaller pieces before it started. I set up a build pipeline with automated tests and a staging environment, and brought our tester into planning instead of at the end. Rather than hand down a process, I ran short retrospectives where the team changed how we worked, and we started with small features to build confidence.
scenarios.result: Within a year the team released every fortnight, and the process was one the team owned and kept improving.
measurableResults: From about three releases a year to one every two weeks

scenarios.title: Started sitting with users to find out what they really needed
scenarios.situation: Almost every feature we shipped was followed straight away by requests to add something missing or change how it behaved. We were building what people asked for, not what they needed.
scenarios.task: Understand requirements well enough, before development, that features landed right the first time.
scenarios.action: I began sitting with the people who had asked for each feature, watching how they worked and asking what they were trying to achieve rather than what they wanted built. I used that to rewrite specifications before development started, and checked the draft back with them.
scenarios.result: Features needed far less rework, my manager noticed the change, and the people we built for started giving much more positive feedback on new releases.

scenarios.title: Took over a fixed-price client build that had overrun badly
scenarios.situation: A fixed-price build for a client had been sold as about three weeks of work. When I took it over, two developers had spent five months on it and it was still far from done, because the client's expectations had grown well beyond what was sold.
scenarios.task: Find out where the project really stood and get it to an outcome both the client and the company could accept.
scenarios.action: I reviewed the code and the original agreement side by side and listed what had been promised against what was being asked for. I took that gap to my director first, then went through it with the client in plain terms. Together we agreed a smaller first release and a new contract for the rest. I wrote the core of the remaining work myself so the other two developers could go back to their own projects.
scenarios.result: The client signed the revised scope, the first release shipped, and the rest was delivered under the new contract. The team's other work carried on without further disruption.
measurableResults: A three-week estimate had grown to five months of work by two developers

scenarios.title: Untangled an architecture debate by agreeing what our words meant
scenarios.situation: Another developer and I were redesigning a notifications service to be event-driven. Our discussions kept going round in circles and getting tense, even though we seemed to agree on the goal.
scenarios.task: Break the deadlock so the redesign could move forward.
scenarios.action: I stepped back from the design itself and noticed we used the same words, like "subscription" and "channel", for different things. We wrote a short glossary together, split each overloaded term into separate concepts, and drew the boundaries between the processes and the data each one owned.
scenarios.result: Once we shared a vocabulary the disagreement disappeared, and the redesign moved on quickly.

scenarios.title: Proposed retiring a legacy add-on that was draining the team
scenarios.situation: We still maintained an on-premise reporting add-on that had once sold well. Most customers had moved to building their own reports, it was hard to keep running on new platforms, and after the team shrank it took a steady share of our time for little return.
scenarios.task: Decide whether the add-on was still worth keeping, and what to do about the customers still using it.
scenarios.action: I pulled together what it cost us in support and maintenance against what it earned, and proposed retiring it rather than carrying on with a split focus. I worked with the commercial team to agree the decision and a timeline, contacted each remaining customer, and wrote hand-over documentation for those who wanted to run it themselves.
scenarios.result: The add-on was retired in an orderly way once existing commitments were met, and the time it had taken went back into the main product.
